title: Calculus 3: Multivariable and Vector Calculus
semester: 15-week semester · 12 instructional units · Weeks 13–15 synthesis, review, and assessment
description: A coherent semester of three-dimensional geometry, vector-valued functions, multivariable differentiation and optimization, multiple integration, and the major theorems of vector calculus.
outcomes: Use vectors, dot products, and cross products to analyze geometric relationships and equations of lines, planes, and surfaces in three dimensions.
Differentiate vector-valued and multivariable functions and interpret velocities, partial derivatives, gradients, directional derivatives, and linear approximations.
Locate and classify unconstrained extrema and solve constrained optimization problems using Lagrange multipliers with appropriate geometric justification.
Set up and evaluate double and triple integrals in rectangular, polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates with correctly described bounds.
Evaluate line and surface integrals and connect circulation and flux through Green's, Stokes', and the divergence theorems.
Translate multivariable models into precise notation, verify orientations and domains, and communicate exact calculations and their geometric meanings.

units.title: Three-Dimensional Coordinates and Vector Products
units.summary: Locate points in three-dimensional coordinates and represent displacement with vectors, their components, magnitudes, and unit directions. Use the dot product for lengths, angles, and projections, and the right-handed cross product for normals and area; distinguish scalar outputs from vector outputs and check cross-product order carefully.
objectives: Compute distances, vector magnitudes, and componentwise vector operations in three-dimensional coordinates.
Evaluate dot products and use them to determine angles, orthogonality, and scalar projections.
Evaluate cross products with correct right-hand orientation and interpret their magnitudes geometrically.

units.title: Lines, Planes, and Quadric Surfaces
units.summary: Build parametric equations for lines from a point and direction, and scalar equations for planes from a point and normal vector. Relate intersections and distances to vector products, then recognize spheres, cylinders, paraboloids, ellipsoids, cones, and hyperboloids from their equations and traces without confusing axis orientation.
objectives: Construct and evaluate parametric line equations and determine where lines meet planes.
Use normal vectors and point-normal equations to compute distances and describe planes.
Recognize standard quadric surfaces and use completing the square and coordinate traces to identify their geometry.

units.title: Vector-Valued Motion and Arc Length
units.summary: Treat a space curve as a vector-valued function and differentiate component by component to obtain velocity and acceleration. Interpret speed as the magnitude of velocity, and compute arc length by integrating speed; keep parameter intervals explicit and distinguish the position vector from its scalar derivative quantities.
objectives: Differentiate vector-valued functions componentwise and evaluate velocity and acceleration at specified parameters.
Compute speed from velocity components and explain its relationship to the direction of motion.
Set up and evaluate arc-length integrals over stated parameter intervals, simplifying speed before integrating.

units.title: Multivariable Functions, Limits, and Partial Derivatives
units.summary: Describe domains and level sets of functions of several variables, then evaluate limits by substitution when continuity applies. Investigate questionable limits along different paths, remembering that one path never proves existence, and introduce partial derivatives by differentiating with respect to one variable while treating every other independent variable as constant.
objectives: Determine domain restrictions and evaluate multivariable functions and continuous limits at specified points.
Use path-dependent values to demonstrate that a two-variable limit does not exist.
Compute first partial derivatives while correctly treating non-differentiation variables as constants.

units.title: Chain Rule, Linearization, and Differentials
units.summary: Apply the multivariable chain rule by tracking every path through which the selected independent variable affects the output, including intermediate variables that depend on several parameters. Form tangent-plane linearizations and use differentials for nearby estimates, honoring the base point and signed increments rather than substituting into only one branch.
objectives: Construct dependence diagrams and apply the chain rule for one or several independent variables.
Compute linearizations at a base point and use them to estimate nearby function values.
Evaluate total differentials with signed increments and interpret them as first-order changes.

units.title: Gradients, Directional Derivatives, and Tangent Planes
units.summary: Combine partial derivatives into the gradient and compute directional derivatives by dotting with a unit direction. Interpret the gradient as normal to a level surface and as the direction of steepest increase, then use that normal vector to write tangent planes and check orientation, scaling, and evaluation points.
objectives: Evaluate gradient components and the magnitude of the gradient at specified points.
Compute directional derivatives using a given unit vector and interpret maximum rates of change.
Construct tangent planes to explicit and implicit surfaces using gradient normal vectors.

units.title: Unconstrained Optimization and Classification
units.summary: Find interior critical points by solving the simultaneous zero-gradient equations and include points where derivatives fail to exist when relevant. Classify nondegenerate critical points with the second-derivative discriminant, while checking function values and global behavior separately; a positive discriminant alone does not distinguish a minimum from a maximum.
objectives: Solve simultaneous partial-derivative equations to locate critical points of two-variable functions.
Compute the second-derivative discriminant and use it with the sign of fₓₓ to classify local extrema and saddles.
Evaluate candidate points and reason about quadratic global behavior when determining extreme values.

units.title: Lagrange Multipliers and Constrained Optimization
units.summary: Optimize a function subject to a smooth constraint by solving ∇f = λ∇g together with g = constant, then compare all candidate values and any boundary behavior. Interpret the multiplier through normal-vector alignment, avoid omitting the constraint equation, and use symmetry only after verifying that it follows from the system.
objectives: Set up complete Lagrange systems including the original constraint and solve for all relevant candidates.
Compare candidate function values to determine constrained maxima and minima.
Interpret Lagrange normal-vector alignment and the role of λ in representative optimization problems.

units.title: Double Integrals and Polar Coordinates
units.summary: Interpret double integrals as accumulated signed volume or mass and evaluate them iteratively with limits matched to the differential order. Sketch regions before reversing integration, convert radially symmetric regions to polar coordinates with dA = r dr dθ, and use area or averaging to normalize angular factors when requested.
objectives: Evaluate iterated double integrals while preserving the correct order of limits and differentials.
Describe two-dimensional regions and reverse integration order without changing their boundary inequalities.
Evaluate double integrals and average values using polar coordinates, including the Jacobian factor r.

units.title: Triple Integrals in Rectangular, Cylindrical, and Spherical Coordinates
units.summary: Build triple integrals from nested spatial inequalities, keeping projection regions and cross-sectional heights consistent with the chosen order. Convert cylindrical coordinates with dV = r dz dr dθ and spherical coordinates with dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ, distinguishing polar angle φ from azimuth θ and using volume-normalized averages where appropriate.
objectives: Evaluate triple integrals over boxes and regions bounded by planes with correct nested limits.
Set up cylindrical-coordinate integrals using consistent axial heights, radial bounds, and the Jacobian r.
Set up spherical-coordinate integrals with ρ² sin φ and compute volume-normalized average values.

units.title: Vector Fields, Line Integrals, and Green's Theorem
units.summary: Evaluate scalar line integrals with ds = ||r′(t)||dt and work or circulation integrals with dr = r′(t)dt, preserving the parameter's orientation for the latter. Recognize conservative fields through potentials, and apply Green's theorem only to positively oriented closed planar curves with the correct P, Q convention and enclosed region.
objectives: Compute scalar and vector line integrals from explicit parametrizations with appropriate differential elements.
Use potential functions to evaluate path-independent work integrals between stated endpoints.
Apply Green's theorem to positively oriented closed curves and verify the sign from counterclockwise traversal.

units.title: Curl, Divergence, Surface Integrals, Stokes', and Divergence Theorems
units.summary: Compute curl and divergence as vector and scalar differential measures, then evaluate oriented surface integrals for circulation density and flux. Connect boundary circulation to surface curl through Stokes' theorem and outward closed-surface flux to integrated divergence, checking normal orientation, boundary compatibility, and the sign of every conversion.
objectives: Compute components of curl and point values of divergence for three-dimensional vector fields.
Evaluate oriented surface flux by converting a closed-surface integral to a triple integral of divergence.
Apply Stokes' theorem with compatible curve and normal orientations and distinguish its role from the divergence theorem.
